To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the fit between mHealth tools and the healthcare tasks they are intended to facilitate, is a critical determinant of their utilization and subsequent impacts on CHW's performance.

mHealth tools have the potential to improve CHW's performance, but this potential will only be realized if the tools are adequately designed and fit the intended purpose of healthcare service delivery.
mHealth tools are a viable solution for improving healthcare service delivery outcomes in Kenya.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the utilization of mhealth technology by CHW's and how it impacts their performance in the delivery of health care services to their clients.
understanding the determinants of the utilization of m-health tools and their impact on the performance of community health workers (CHWs) in Kenya.

the development of a replicable, generalizable, and scalable TPC framework to examine perceptions of task technology, and subsequent impacts of utilization on CHW's performance in the developing country context of Kenya.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

this study will contribute towards the enhancement of community health service delivery systems, empowerment of CHW’s in the delivery of health services, and improved scalability of mHealth deployments, through the development of a Technology to Performance Chain model, which will be used to study the perceptions of task technology, utilization and performance of CHW’s, in Kenya.
This study aims to examine the fit (from four fit perspectives) between health care tasks and mHealth technology tools used by CHWs in Kenya.

this study will contribute towards the development of an evidence based solution to improve the effectiveness of mHealth initiatives in developing countries by (1) providing empirical evidence into the utilization and effects of mHealth tools on the workflow efficiencies of Community Health Workers, and (2) providing a replicable model for the assessment of the fit of healthcare tasks and mhealth tools.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are trying to answer questions like: What are the factors influencing CHWs' perceptions of the fit between their work tasks and mobile technology tools?
we are developing a model to understand the impact of technology on performance in community health work settings.
this study aims to develop and validate an extended TPC model to explain CHW utilization of mobile health tools and the performance impacts of such utilization.
The main takeaway from our work is that

mHealth initiatives can only be effective if they are designed with the specific needs and requirements of their intended users, and are deployed in a manner that is consistent with the workflows of their end users.

the use of mobile technology enabled healthcare service delivery tools for CHW's can have a significant impact on CHW performance in Kenya, and that the TPC model is a valid and reliable framework for examining the fit of mhealth tools to CHW's work tasks.
we have developed a theoretical framework to study mHealth tool utilization in the developing world context.
